lessons.culture: Family is central in Yemeni society, and asking about family members is an important part of any greeting. People usually ask directly where relatives live and often discuss family plans. Saying you are still single is a straightforward answer, often followed by "إن شاء الله" (God willing).

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "عندك عايلة كبيرة؟" Say yes, you have a brother and two sisters.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Yemeni speech uses "عندي" and "أخوي".

exercises.tip: "عندي" is the everyday way to say what you have, including family.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "My mother."

too_formal.feedback: This is the formal written term; everyday Yemeni speech says "أمي".

exercises.tip: "أمي" and "أبوي" are the everyday words for mother and father.

exercises.tip: The ending "-وي" here means "my" on top of "أبو".

exercises.prompt: Which word means "my sister"?

too_formal.feedback: This is a more formal word for sister than the everyday "أختي".

exercises.tip: "أخوي" is brother, "أختي" is sister.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "عندي أخوي و_____." Meaning: I have a brother and two sisters.

exercises.tip: "-ين" makes the dual: "أخت" becomes "أختين" for two sisters.

exercises.tip: "لسع" means "still" and is used constantly in everyday Yemeni speech.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "my husband"?

too_formal.feedback: "الزوج" is the word for husband in general; "زوجي" is "my husband".

exercises.tip: "زوجي" is husband, "مرتي" is wife.

exercises.tip: "ولد" is the everyday word for son in Yemeni Arabic.

exercises.tip: "كم أنتم" ("how many are you") is the everyday way to ask about family size.

exercises.tip: A short place-name answer is enough in casual speech.

lessons.culture: Food and hospitality are central to Yemeni culture. Coffee is always offered to guests, and refusing it can be seen as impolite. "نُعيماً" is said after someone finishes eating or drinking, and "بِالْعَافِيَة" is said while eating; both receive the blessing "الله يَعْطِيك الْعَافِيَة" (May God give you well-being). Meals often last a long time with lots of conversation.

exercises.tip: "جوعان" for a man, "جوعانة" for a woman.

exercises.tip: "أشتي" plus a verb is the everyday pattern for "I want to...".

exercises.tip: "نُعيماً" comes after eating or drinking; "بِالْعَافِيَة" comes while the meal is still going.

exercises.tip: "بِالْعَافِيَة" and "الله يَعْطِيك الْعَافِيَة" are a fixed pair, always said together.

exercises.prompt: Someone says "نُعيماً" to you after you finish eating. Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is a generic formal thanks rather than the fixed spoken reply "الله يَعْطِيك الْعَافِيَة".

exercises.tip: "نُعيماً" and "الله يَعْطِيك الْعَافِيَة" are a fixed pair, said after eating or drinking.

exercises.tip: "الحساب" is the everyday word for the bill at a restaurant.

exercises.tip: Question word first is natural: "إيش + تحب + تاكل؟"

exercises.tip: "جوعان" is hungry, "عطشان" is thirsty.

pair.english: How old are you? (to a man)

lessons.culture: In Yemen it is ordinary to ask a man his age, his work and where his family lives, and a mention of children is met with "ما شاء الله، الله يحفظهم". Family ties are strong: a father's brother's son (ولد عمي) is treated almost like a brother, and the oldest brother (الكبير) is often the one the family looks to.

exercises.tip: "ساكنين" is the plural of "ساكن" (living), because you speak of the whole family.

exercises.tip: "-ين" at the end makes the dual, like "أختين" (two sisters).

lessons.culture: A Yemeni family usually eats around one "سفرة" laid on the floor or the table, with shared dishes, and the host keeps insisting that guests take more. Breakfast is called "الصبوح", and after the meal the host is thanked with "الله يعطيك العافية" and answers "بالعافية" or "نعيماً".

pair.english: Where do you live? (to a man)

lessons.culture: In Yemen people usually name their "حارة" (the quarter they live in), such as حدة in Sana'a, rather than a street number, and many families who live in the city still go back to their village for the feasts. Neighbours are close, they greet each other every day, and "الجار قبل الدار" (the neighbour before the house) is a saying you will hear.

lessons.culture: Yemeni houses are often tall, with several floors (أدوار), and the "مفرج" is the reception room where the family and guests sit, usually on the top floor with a view. When a guest praises your home you answer "الله يبارك فيك", and the host says "البيت بيتك" (the house is yours).

lessons.culture: In a Yemeni home the guest is shown first to the "مفرج" or the guest room, and the host says "البيت بيتك" (the house is yours). exercises.tip: The "مفرج" is the main sitting room where the family and guests gather.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Go to the garden." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "روح البستان".

exercises.tip: To a woman: "روحي البستان".

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "Where are the stairs?"
exercises.tip: "وين" starts every "where" question.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "upstairs"?
exercises.tip: "فوق" is above or upstairs, "تحت" is below or downstairs.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "نطلع / يالله / على / السطح"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "يالله نطلع".

exercises.tip: "يالله" means "let's go" and "نطلع" is "we go up".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "جنب / البلكونة / غرفة / النوم"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "بلكونة" and "جنب".

exercises.tip: "جنب" means "next to".

lessons.culture: In Yemen, "أبشر" is the warm way to say "right away, gladly" when someone asks you for something, and a guest who needs anything in the house is never too shy to ask. Power cuts are common in Yemen, so many homes keep a lamp or a small solar light to hand, and "طفي الضوء" and "شغل الضوء" are the two commands you will hear most at night.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "وين الريموت؟" Say it is on the sofa.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "على الكنبة".

exercises.tip: "كنبة" is the everyday word for sofa.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "وين المفتاح؟" Say it is on the table.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "على الطاولة".

exercises.tip: "طاولة" is the table.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "أحتاج بطانية." Answer that you will bring one gladly.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "أبشر".

exercises.tip: "أبشر" literally means "be glad" and is the usual answer to a request.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "الغسالة ما تشتغل." Say tomorrow we will fix it.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "بكرة" for tomorrow.

exercises.tip: "بكرة" is tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "شغل _____." Meaning: Switch on the light.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "شغل الضوء".

exercises.tip: "شغل" is the usual verb for switching something on.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "المراية جنب _____." Meaning: The mirror is next to the door.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "مراية" and "جنب".

exercises.tip: "جنب" means "next to".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I need a blanket."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "أحتاج بطانية" or "أبغى بطانية" (I want a blanket).

exercises.tip: Both "أحتاج" (I need) and "أبغى" (I want) are used for asking for something.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Open the window." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: "نافذة" is the formal word for window; everyday speech says "شباك".

exercises.tip: "شباك" is the everyday word for window.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "Switch off the light"?
exercises.tip: "طفي" is switch off, "شغل" is switch on.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "fan"?
exercises.tip: "مروحة" is the fan; you "شغل" it.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "الغرفة / سرير / في / فيه"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "فيه" for "there is".

exercises.tip: "فيه" means "there is".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "تشتغل / الغسالة / ما"

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Yemeni speech says "ما تشتغل".

exercises.tip: "ما" before the verb makes it negative.

challenge.title: Meeting Family Over a Meal
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Yemeni Arabic conversation that lasts at least 10 lines. It must include a question about someone's family, a description of at least one relative, a statement of hunger or thirst, ordering or offering food and drink, the fixed exchange بالهنا / الله يهنيك or صحتين / عليك التمام, and asking for the bill. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 2 and include both a masculine-address form and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: A question about family using عندك عايلة؟ or كم أنتم في العايلة؟
A description of at least one family member using أمي, أبوي, أخوي, أختي, زوجي, مرتي, ولدي, or بنتي.
A statement of hunger or thirst using جوعان, جوعانة, or عطشان.
An order or offer of food or drink using أشتي آكل or أشتي اشرب.
The fixed exchange بِالْعَافِيَة / الله يَعْطِيك الْعَافِيَة, or نُعيماً / الله يَعْطِيك الْعَافِيَة.
A request for the bill using الحساب لو سمحت or كم الحساب؟
Both a masculine-address form (such as عندك) and a feminine-address form (such as عندك).
